web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Products, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
question: What does this company sell, to whom, and how much of its revenue rests on one molecule and one supplier country?

epigraph.quote: Our revenue from operations depends on one product i.e. “R-32”.
epigraph.author: Stallion Red Herring Prospectus, risk factors, 11 January 2025 [6]

web_blocks.html: The company describes four product families on its website: equipment and spares for the air-conditioning and refrigeration industry, refrigerants and fluorines, semiconductor and electronics specialty gases, and consumer refrigerants and related products [13]. That list is how management presents the business. The money, however, is concentrated in a few places, and the audited accounts do not show you which.

The audited statement of profit and loss shows revenue from operations as a single line [1]. There is no product-level segment split in the audited notes I checked. The MD&A also labels ₹434.12 crore as revenue from operations, but that figure is total income: audited revenue of ₹430.68 crore plus other income of ₹3.45 crore [2][1]. When a report calls the company a specialty-gas business, check which product is actually generating the money. The mix below comes from the RHP and from management’s remarks, not from the audited notes.

The first family on the website, equipment and spares for air-conditioning and refrigeration, does not show up in the filed numbers. The RHP concentration figures do not separate it, and the sources I read give it no share of revenue. Treat it as part of the company’s shop window rather than as a measured earnings line.

web_blocks.takeaway: Each row points the same way. Refrigerant gases are the bulk of product sales, the company depends on imports for most of its input cost, and ten customers account for three-quarters of revenue. The source is the RHP risk-factor section [6][25].

web_blocks.title: R-32: the product that carries the company

web_blocks.html: R-32 is a refrigerant used in air conditioners. The RHP says the company’s revenue depends on it, in plain terms, and that any fall in demand for it could hurt sales, earnings and cash flow [6]. That is the single biggest concentration in the business. The company’s plan is to make some of it rather than only buy and blend it. The August 2026 call put the planned Bhilwara R-32 plant at 10,000 metric tons, and management described the plant as the first major backward integration [8][2].

The plant has a cash-flow effect that management has repeatedly revised. In August 2026, management said the earlier FY27 contribution of about ₹250 crore would “change a little bit” [9]. By the 19 November 2026 Q2 FY27 earnings call, management confirmed that Bhilwara R-32 trials will conclude by March 2027, phased production starts April 2027, and 100% stabilization is expected by May 2027—reducing FY27 R-32 revenue contribution to zero [36]. For FY28, management now projects 7,000 tonnes of output contributing ₹350 to ₹400 crore (alongside ₹600 crore at full utilization in an illustrative ₹1,200 crore steady-state mix) [36]. Crucially, Bhilwara Phase 1 excludes upstream anhydrous hydrofluoric acid (AHF) manufacturing, leaving Stallion reliant on external AHF purchases without long-term contracts [6][36].

web_blocks.html: A product map is only useful if you can tie each line to a site and a verified status. The table below updates the FY26 annual report and August 2026 call with the November 2026 Q2 FY27 disclosures, CARE Ratings IPO monitoring report, and Infomerics rights-issue monitoring report [36][37][38].

web_blocks.takeaway: Khalapur helium is now operational (334 days behind its IPO target) [37], but both Bhilwara R-32 and Mambattu have slipped again into FY28 with zero FY27 revenue and cost overruns, while HFO construction is pushed past R-32 stabilization [36][37][38].

web_blocks.html: The product map matters most for margin, and management refined its illustrative mix on the 19 November 2026 call [36]. On a hypothetical ₹1,200 crore turnover, management projected ₹600 crore from Bhilwara R-32 at a 22% PAT margin, ₹200 crore from HFO blends and helium at 15% PAT, and ₹400 crore from the regular refrigerant business at 10% PAT (lifting to 15% only if post-2028 quotas restrict imports) [36]. That is lower than the August 2026 remark that newer lines would run at 24% PAT [9], and all three newer pillars remain unproven in audited accounts while core refrigerant gases still carry the business today [25].

Put the two sources of margin side by side. The core business is still doing the heavy lifting today, and in Q2 FY27 its operating spread compressed sharply even before non-cash ESOP accounting [36]. Whether backward integration lifts consolidated margins depends on Bhilwara starting smoothly and competing profitably against larger integrated domestic producers.

web_blocks.title: Backward-integrated rivals and the domestic R-32 capacity surge

web_blocks.html: A crucial blind spot in reading Stallion solely through its own filings is what India’s backward-integrated fluorochemical majors—SRF, Gujarat Fluorochemicals (GFL), and Navin Fluorine (NFIL)—delivered in the exact same Q2 FY27 (July–September 2026) quarter [42][43][44]. While Stallion’s core operating margin (ex-ESOP and ex-other income) fell to 9.19% (2.20% reported) [14][36], Navin Fluorine grew Q2 FY27 revenue 57% year on year to ₹1,191 crore and profit 81% to ₹269 crore at a 34.2% EBITDA margin, commencing commercial R-32 output at Surat (15,000 MTPA HFC capacity) and extending its HFO supply contract with Solstice Advanced Materials (~$590 million) through December 2032 [42]. Gujarat Fluorochemicals grew Q2 FY27 revenue 45.5% to ₹1,760 crore—with fluorochemicals up 135% year on year on R-32—at a 26.9% EBITDA margin [43]. SRF grew Q2 FY27 revenue 35% to ₹4,904 crore, earning ₹527.8 crore of Chemicals EBIT (25.4% margin) while building a 20,000 MTPA fourth-generation refrigerant unit, a 30,000 MTPA AHF plant, and over 65,000 MTPA of HFC capacity in Odisha [44].

The divergence exposes a structural disadvantage. On the 19 November 2026 call, Stallion’s own CEO acknowledged that India’s domestic R-32 demand is roughly 20,000 tonnes per year while coming domestic installed capacity reaches about 80,000 tonnes—four times domestic demand [36]. Integrated incumbents already own upstream AHF capacity, decades of fluorine process engineering, and global export channels [42][43][44]. Stallion enters late, without captive AHF in Bhilwara Phase 1, and holds only a non-exclusive Honeywell distribution relationship while HFO patents approach expiry—meaning larger rivals can compete directly across both R-32 and next-generation HFOs [36].

web_blocks.title: How the business works, end to end

web_blocks.html: The chain is simple to describe. The company buys its raw material, much of it imported, then debulks, blends, bottles and sells refrigerant gases to air-conditioning and refrigeration customers. The planned plants move one step further up the chain. Instead of buying and blending R-32 and HFO, the company would make them. Each step up should earn more per kilogram if it works—provided external AHF input costs and domestic R-32 oversupply do not compress the manufacturing spread. That is the thesis behind the capital spending examined in chapter 3.

web_blocks.title: What the filings do not split

web_blocks.html: No filed number gives the revenue of the helium project, of R-32, or of the distribution business on its own. The audited revenue line is one figure, and the RHP gives broad percentages. Even after Khalapur helium started on 21 September 2026, Q2 FY27 filings still report a single reportable segment (manufacture of industrial gases) with no product-level margin split [36][37]. Use management’s plant-level projections strictly as targets to verify against future filings.

web_blocks.title: Helium: the second product family, and a different supply chain

web_blocks.html: The Khalapur facility is the company’s helium project, with an installed capacity of 1,200 metric tons a year. Commercial operations commenced on 21 September 2026 (recorded as completed 29 September 2026 in CARE Ratings’ monitoring report), moving the project from construction into early ramp-up [36][37]. Liquid helium is sourced under a partnership with Sharjah Oxygen Company in Dubai, which sources from RAS Gases & Oilfields in Qatar [1]. On the August 2026 call, management forecast a two-to-three-year helium shortfall [8], guided to roughly 20% utilization of the 1,200 metric tons in year one rather than 50%, and noted helium rates near ₹4,000 a kilogram [9]. Capacity is not output, and the November 2026 disclosures provided no initial revenue or volume run-rate [36].

Helium is a different kind of business from refrigerant gas. In October 2025 management explained that helium is not manufactured by anyone. It is recovered as a by-product, then refined and liquefied, and the company’s role is in processing and handling [11]. That makes the helium project a logistics and purification business whose inputs depend on a few producing countries, which is the point the next chapter tests.

The helium supply link runs through a partnership with Sharjah Oxygen Company in Dubai, which sources liquid helium from RAS Gases & Oilfields in Qatar. The annual report calls it a long-term strategic partnership [1]. The contract terms are not in the sources, so I cannot say how long it runs or what share of supply it covers. That is the first thing to ask about any helium revenue number.

web_blocks.title: Customers and the cost of concentration

web_blocks.html: Ten customers accounted for 77.32% of revenue in the six months to September 2024, against 72.88% in FY22 [6]. The top two customers alone were 35.34% of revenue in FY24 [6]. Concentration of that size is not unusual in industrial supply, but it changes what a lost order means. A single large customer taking volume elsewhere moves the whole revenue line, not a slice of it.

The top-ten share has risen in every period the RHP reports, from 72.88% in FY22 to 74.77% in FY23, 75.69% in FY24 and 77.32% in the six months to September 2024 [6]. That can be normal for an industrial supplier, but it means the business is more exposed to its largest buyers each year. That is the direction to watch.

The arithmetic of the top two is blunt. In the six months to September 2024 the top two customers were 30.66% of revenue and the top ten 77.32% [6]. That leaves about 23% of revenue for every other buyer combined. A decision by one of the top two to cut volume or move a contract would reach about a third of the company’s sales in one move. The sources I checked do not give the length of those relationships.

Put the chapter in one sentence. The company sells mainly refrigerant gas, buys most of its input from abroad, depends on a small group of buyers, has just commissioned a helium unit, and is building a delayed, non-AHF-integrated R-32 plant into a domestic market where integrated giants are expanding capacity to four times local demand.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
paragraphs: Ask yourself which part of this business you would own if the company disappeared tomorrow. The answer is R-32 distribution and blending, a newly started helium processing line with no disclosed volume yet, a heavily concentrated customer list, and two delayed capex projects still waiting for FY28 commissioning. Each is a real asset, and each carries execution risk.

The peer check is the sobering lens. When backward-integrated peers like Navin Fluorine, Gujarat Fluorochemicals, and SRF earn 25% to 34% operating margins in the same quarter that Stallion’s core margin slips below 10%, the gap is not bad luck—it is the structural difference between making base fluorine molecules with captive AHF and importing finished gas to blend.

book_paragraphs: Let me describe what the company sells, because the words on the website are broader than the money. There are four product families: equipment and spares for air conditioning and refrigeration, refrigerants and fluorines, semiconductor and specialty gases, and consumer refrigerants. That is a wide shop window. But when you look at the filed numbers, refrigerant gases are the bulk of product sales. In the six months to September 2024 they were about 87% of product revenue.

The most important thing in this chapter is one sentence from the Red Herring Prospectus. The company said plainly that its revenue depends on one product, R-32. R-32 is a refrigerant used in air conditioners. If demand for it falls, or the company loses its position in it, the business has very little else to fall back on. That is the reason the planned plant at Bhilwara matters. The company wants to make R-32 rather than only buy, debulk and blend it—though notably without upstream AHF manufacturing in Phase 1.

The audited statements do not split revenue by product, and that is worth knowing. Even in the Q2 FY27 results filed in November 2026, Stallion reported a single reportable segment. So when someone tells you what share of profit comes from helium or from the new plant, ask them where the number comes from. In this report I have used the RHP, monitoring reports, and transcripts, and I have labelled each figure with its source.

The helium project at Khalapur is a different kind of business. Commercial operations began on 21 September 2026 at the 1,200 metric tonne facility—334 days after the original October 2025 IPO prospectus target, per CARE Ratings. Helium is not manufactured by anyone; it is recovered as a by-product, refined, and liquefied. So Stallion is a purifier and handler dependent on its Dubai-Qatar supply link, not an owner of a resource. Management guided to about 20% utilization in year one and has not yet disclosed initial commercial volumes.

Customer concentration is the other half of the picture. Ten customers made up about three-quarters of revenue in the six months to September 2024. The top two were about 35% of revenue in FY24. In a business like this, a large customer is a relationship that matters, and a lost order moves the whole revenue line. You want to know how that concentration is changing over time, and the filings have still not updated the ratio.

Now look at the updated plant map as of November 2026. Stallion now lists five operating sites: Panvel, Manesar, Ghiloth, legacy Khalapur, and the newly started Khalapur helium unit. The two growth plants behind the transformation thesis have both slipped into FY28. Bhilwara R-32 is now guided for March 2027 trials, phased April production, and May stabilization—a seven-month delay versus the rights-issue schedule, with zero FY27 revenue and a 40 crore cost overrun for over 90 ISO-tank containers and equipment. Mambattu was redesigned across its full acreage, nearly doubling its cost scope and pushing completion to January 2027 or Q1 FY28, also with zero FY27 revenue. Meanwhile, the planned Bhilwara HFO plant still awaits environmental clearance and will not start construction until three to five months after R-32 stabilizes.

Management refined its illustrative margin mix on the 19 November 2026 call. On a hypothetical 1,200 crore revenue base, it modelled 600 crore from Bhilwara at a 22% PAT margin, 200 crore from HFO blends and helium at 15%, and 400 crore from regular distribution at 10%—rising to 15% only if post-2028 import quotas tighten supply. Those are slightly more modest on helium and HFO than the 24% figure floated in August, and every rupee of manufacturing margin remains unproven until reactors run smoothly.

Now place Stallion beside its Indian peers in the exact same July–September 2026 quarter, because this is what the original analysis under-examined. While Stallion’s core operating margin ex-ESOP and ex-other income fell to 9.19%, Navin Fluorine grew revenue 57% to 1,191 crore at a 34.2% EBITDA margin while commissioning 15,000 tonnes of HFC/R-32 capacity and extending its Solstice HFO contract through 2032. Gujarat Fluorochemicals grew fluorochemicals 135% on R-32 with a 26.9% consolidated EBITDA margin, and SRF earned a 25.4% Chemicals EBIT margin while building 20,000 tonnes of fourth-generation refrigerants and 30,000 tonnes of captive AHF in Odisha.

That peer gap is structural, not cyclical noise. On the 19 November 2026 call, Stallion’s own CEO noted that India’s R-32 demand is about 20,000 tonnes against 80,000 tonnes of coming domestic capacity—four times local demand. Unlike SRF, GFL, and Navin Fluorine, Stallion is entering without captive AHF integration, with a non-exclusive Honeywell tie-up, and into a market where larger integrated manufacturers already dominate exports and next-generation HFO contracts.

Here is a practical way to hold all of this. Picture the company as three businesses sitting on one balance sheet: a volatile imported-refrigerant blending business carrying the company today; a delayed, non-AHF-integrated R-32 plant facing domestic overcapacity when it starts in FY28; and a newly commissioned helium unit still awaiting proof of commercial volume. Each carries a very different risk profile.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Ask which part of this business you would still own if the refrigerant line stopped growing tomorrow. The honest answer is that the company is most valuable in a case where R-32 keeps working and the new plant arrives on time. That is a narrow path, and it is worth stating in your own words before you read the next chapters.
